PacTrans 2026 · Session 1B · Washington State University

Bridge-Specific Deep Learning for Deterioration Forecasting: A Geography-Aware HyperNetwork for Pacific Northwest Bridges

Every bridge deserves its own forecast.

HyperNetwork: a model that builds bridge-specific forecasters.

Haifeng Wang

Assistant Professor · Civil and Environmental Engineering
Washington State University

University of Alaska Anchorage · October 9, 2026PacTrans Small Project
Thank you to PacTrans and our hosts at the University of Alaska Anchorage. I am Haifeng Wang from Washington State University. Every bridge ages in its own way, so each deserves its own forecast. Deep learning means learning patterns from many examples. Our HyperNetwork is a model that builds a forecasting model for each bridge. I will explain the question, the idea, our tests, the findings, and what they mean for practice. Alaska will help us see how national learning supports small data. Let me start with the decision that makes this work matter.

Background · The stakes

A forecast helps decide where bridge repair money goes.

WA · OR · ID · AK

Forecast accuracy helps guide repair timing

Sources: ASCE, 2025 Report Card for America's Infrastructure; Region 10 dataset audit.

A forecast helps decide when to repair a bridge and where to direct funding. The United States has about six hundred seventeen thousand highway bridges. More than forty two thousand need structural attention, and the ASCE 2025 Report Card puts repair needs at about one hundred ninety one billion dollars. Our Region 10 records contain twenty two thousand one hundred seventy eight bridges. The deck is the surface that carries the road. Here, earlier ratings are in ink, our smaller model's regional forecast is in crimson, and later actual ratings are open circles. This Oregon bridge was excluded from training. Its forecast error is nearest the middle of the declining-bridge examples, using the recorded bridge identifier to resolve the tie. The forecast stays near seven as the later actual ratings move to six. (Click.) Forecast accuracy helps guide repair timing and bridge funding.

Background · Region 10

Bridges face different conditions across Region 10.

  • Coast: salt exposure.
  • Inland: freezing and thawing.
  • Alaska: 1,619 bridges.
    The least number of samples in this study.

Source: Region 10 National Bridge Inventory (NBI), the national bridge records. Map locates 22,170 of the 22,178 bridges.

Region 10 brings Washington, Oregon, Idaho, and Alaska into one study. The National Bridge Inventory, or NBI, is the national collection of bridge records. Color shows each bridge's latest deck rating. Alaska has its own map scale. (Click.) Along the coast, engineers consider salt exposure. (Click.) Inland, they consider freezing and thawing. (Click.) Alaska has the least number of samples in this study, with sixteen hundred nineteen bridges. How can bridges across these states learn together while keeping what makes each different?

Question · Shared forecasting rules

Shared forecasting rules offer a starting point.

Steel girder
Inland, near Boise
Steel girder
One Markov chain table
for steel girders

Same material × bridge type

  • Markov chain: a table of chances that ratings change.
    Shared by material and bridge type; starts from the current rating.
  • Plain LSTM: a model that learns from rating histories, with shared settings.
    Ratings, age, traffic and type enter; location does not.

How can location help shape the forecast?

Our versions of the comparison methods. Plain LSTM follows Miao, Yokota and Zhang (2023). Examples and grid are illustrative.

Consider two steel girder bridges, one coastal near Seattle and one inland near Boise. Our Markov chain method uses a table of chances that a bridge rating stays the same or changes. Bridges with the same material and type share that table. The grid here is an illustration. (Click.) Location, age and traffic are outside that table; the current rating sets where a forecast starts. (Click.) Plain LSTM means long short-term memory. It is a model that learns patterns from rating histories. Our version also uses age, truck traffic, material and bridge type. These inputs can give different forecasts, while every bridge uses shared model settings. Location is outside its inputs. (Click.) These methods offer a useful starting point. How can each bridge's location help shape its forecaster?

Main question

A bridge-specific forecaster can learn from shared histories.

Can each bridge get its own forecaster by learning from bridges together?

Two features of our data

  1. Yearly records.At most five yearly rating points.
  2. Small data. Alaska has 1,619 bridges.About one fifth as many bridges as Washington.

Source: Region 10 NBI records, 2020 to 2024, and dataset audit.

Can each bridge get its own forecaster by learning from bridges together? Two features of our data guide that choice. (Click.) First, we have at most five yearly ratings per bridge. Annual reporting can carry an inspection rating forward, so a yearly record need not represent a new inspection. We use the available histories together to learn how bridges age. (Click.) Second, states contribute different amounts of data. Alaska has the least number of samples, with sixteen hundred nineteen bridges, about one fifth as many as Washington. We want shared learning to retain differences in structure and location. That is the role of our HyperNetwork.

Source: Ha, Dai and Le (2017), HyperNetworks; project model implementation.

Start with a bridge profile: what the bridge is and where it is. It includes location, which neither comparison method uses. (Click.) The profile goes into a HyperNetwork learned from the training bridges. (Click.) That model sets up an LSTM for this bridge. Similar profiles can lead to similar settings; location can change those settings. The LSTM reads the rating history. (Click.) It forecasts one, two, and three years ahead. We learn from bridges together, rather than trying to learn each bridge's behavior from its few records alone. Ha, Dai, and Le introduced this idea of a model building another model. Let me show what enters and leaves our version.

A smaller generator gave steadier forecasts: about 2.2 million learned settings instead of 32 million.
Its layers are 10 times narrower; the bridge-specific LSTM stays the same.

Regional weather records: temperature, freezing, rain and snow.
About 62% of entries are gaps. Available values are used; gaps are filled.

Source: project model and evaluation methods. Diagram shows the deck-rating test.

The bridge profile goes through five learning layers to set up its forecaster. We call this part the weight generator because it chooses the model's learned settings. Its layers are now ten times narrower, with fifty one, one hundred two, two hundred four and four hundred nine units. The regional generator has about two point two million learned settings, compared with thirty two million earlier. The generated LSTM stays at one layer and thirty two memory units. It reads the deck, structure and support ratings; this test forecasts the deck rating. The other architecture choices stay the same. (Click.) Regional weather inputs include temperature, freezing, rain and snow. About sixty two percent of entries are gaps, which are filled. Weather's contribution remains a topic for further testing.

Our solution · An engineering rule for learning

Without repair, a rising condition rating adds to training error.

Fit the inspections

Average squared error

+
0.05 × cost for increases

Discourage predicted increases

=
Training score
  • The engineering rule:
    stay at or below the last inspected rating.
  • Respect recorded repairs.
    Exclude those steps from the training adjustment.
  • Check the records.
    Remove rating jumps with no documented reconstruction.

Source: project training method and bridge record checks. The rule discourages increases; it does not prevent them.

The engineering rule is that condition stays the same or declines between repairs. Training uses a score that combines average squared forecast differences with zero point zero five times an adjustment for predicted increases. The adjustment averages positive increases without squaring them. (Click.) A forecast above the last inspected rating also adds to the score. (Click.) Consecutive increases at recorded maintenance or reconstruction steps are outside that part of the adjustment. (Click.) Record checks retain rating changes consistent with the reconstruction history. The rule guides learning, while the model can still produce an increase. The backup case illustration caps increases; accuracy scores and the opening example use forecasts as the models produce them. These curves illustrate the rule.

  • 5 test groups, split by bridge. Test bridges are kept out of training.
    All methods use the same groups: HyperNetwork, Markov chain and Plain LSTM.
  • RMSE: an error score in rating points. Lower is better.
    It gives more weight to larger differences. We check rating changes and recorded locations.

Source: project analysis of NBI 2020 to 2024. Regional models use the same bridge splits.

Our regional records contain twenty two thousand one hundred seventy eight bridges and one hundred one thousand seven hundred forty six yearly records from 2020 to 2024. We observe two years and forecast the next three. Eighty one point five percent of bridges have all five yearly records. For shorter histories, we use the earliest two records and score later records where available. Gaps can change the calendar interval. (Click.) We divide bridges into five groups. Each group takes a turn as the test group and stays out of training. All methods use the same grouping rule. (Click.) RMSE means root mean squared error: an error score in rating points that gives larger differences more weight. Lower is better. Every method repeats the test with three choices of groups and starting settings. The table averages fifteen matched runs for each method.

Would more training data help?
We next learn from bridges across the country.

Source: NBI 2020 to 2024. All methods: mean of 15 runs, 5 test groups × 3 repeats.

Learning from Region 10 alone, the smaller bridge-specific HyperNetwork-LSTM has the lowest average RMSE for all three forecast years. (Click.) Its error is four, eleven and fourteen percent lower than Plain LSTM. The advantage grows with the forecast horizon. A smaller weight generator gave steadier forecasts. Compared with the Markov chain, error is lower in thirteen of fifteen, fourteen of fifteen and fourteen of fifteen paired tests. Every row averages the same fifteen runs: five test groups with three starting settings. (Click.) Would more training data help? We next learn from bridges across the country before adapting to Region 10.

A regional model that starts with national experience

Region 10 bridges removed before national training.

Source: national training data audit. Count is before checking history length. Both stages leave out weather records.

We first learn nationally, then adapt to Region 10. Learning nationally first is called pretraining. We removed Washington, Oregon, Idaho and Alaska before that stage. This leaves four hundred sixty three thousand six hundred forty six bridges in the prepared national data. Training uses bridges with enough history for the sequence. (Click.) The smaller generator learns from profiles and rating histories outside Region 10. (Click.) It then adapts using regional training bridges, a step called fine-tuning. Both stages leave out weather records. Test bridges stay outside both training stages. The national setup uses a different set of bridge details from the regional sweep; we also compare regional and national learning with the same setup in the state experiment.

Region 10 bridges removed before national learning. All methods: mean of 15 runs, 5 test groups × 3 repeats.

Learning nationally and adapting locally gives the lowest error for all three forecast years. The green striped bars show that model. (Click.) Error is five point three, four point five, and three point five percent lower than the Markov chain, and lower in all fifteen paired tests at each year. It is three point four, one point zero, and zero point eight percent lower than our regional model. (Click.) Compared with Plain LSTM, error is seven, twelve and fifteen percent lower. The bridge-specific HyperNetwork-LSTM has lower error at every horizon, with the advantage growing farther ahead. Region 10 bridges were removed before national learning. Every comparison series averages fifteen matched runs. Let us now see how the states respond.

Let us explore this with Region 10 partners.

State results: 1 repeat, 5 test groups; the Alaska gain appears in most groups. Region 10 tab uses the national comparison.

Alaska has the least number of samples, and it gains the most from national data in this experiment. The bars share one scale. At one year, national learning brings Alaska's error to zero point two five six. The right panel shows the change relative to regional training and to the Markov chain. I will select two years, then three: Alaska's reductions are nine, eleven and eight percent relative to regional learning, and nineteen, twenty five and twenty four percent relative to the Markov chain. The gain over regional learning appears in four, four and three of five test groups; versus the Markov chain, in four groups at each year. Washington, Oregon and Idaho have changes within about plus or minus three percent relative to regional learning. I will return to Alaska. (Click.) Small data gains the most here. These state results use one repeat; further repeats will show how stable the pattern is. We welcome Region 10 partners' ideas.

Practice · A path to use

A forecast can help build a list an inspector can use.

A research demonstration.
Ready for discussion with agency partners.

Source: example planning tool using NBI records. Forecast line and shading are illustrative. Engineering judgment remains essential.

An engineer needs to find a bridge, see its history, and inspect its forecast. This figure shows how a planning tool could work. The map and history use bridge records. The red forecast line and shaded area illustrate the display; measured predictions and uncertainty would come from the model. (Click.) This research demonstration operates on its own, ready for discussion with agency partners. An engineer would check inspection records and use professional judgment before deciding on maintenance. That brings us to practical opportunities and the next studies.

Practice · Opportunities and next studies

These forecasts could support agency planning.

For agencies

  1. Bridge-specific models support forecasting.Lowest error for all three forecast years.
  2. National data helps the model learn.Alaska gains most in this comparison.
  3. Multi-year forecasts support planning.Use them alongside inspection records.

Next studies

  • Five annual reporting years.
    Test forecasts over longer periods.
  • About 62% of weather entries are gaps.
    Study how weather affects accuracy.
  • State results use one repeat.
    Test different groups and starting points.

Source: project analysis of NBI 2020 to 2024 and regional climate coverage.

For agencies, I see three opportunities. First, the bridge-specific model has the lowest error for all three forecast years in our comparison. Second, national learning supports small data: Alaska gains the most among our states. Third, forecasts several years ahead can help planners decide which bridges to review, alongside inspection records and engineering judgment. (Click.) Our records cover five annual reporting years, so we plan tests over longer periods. About sixty two percent of regional weather entries are gaps; broader weather records will support that study. State results use one choice of groups and starting settings. Further repeats will show how stable these patterns are.

Takeaways

Every bridge ages differently.
Now each can have its own forecast.

  1. A bridge-specific forecaster.Shared learning, bridge-specific models.
  2. Lowest error for all three forecast years.About 3.5 to 5% lower error than the Markov chain.
  3. Small data gains most from national learning.Alaska shows the largest gain in this comparison.

Next steps

Add 1992 to 2019 records for forecasts farther ahead.

Extend national climate data.

Check costs and benefits for bridge planners.

Release an open Region 10 dataset and toolkit.

Supported by PacTrans, the USDOT Region 10 University Transportation Center · PacTrans Small Project.

First, a shared HyperNetwork builds a forecaster from each bridge's profile. Second, the smaller model with national learning has the lowest error at each forecast year, about three point five to five percent lower error than the Markov chain. Third, small data gains most from national learning in this comparison: Alaska has the least number of samples and the largest gain. Next, we plan longer records, more weather data, economic analysis for bridge planners, and an open dataset and toolkit. The goal is to help engineers connect forecasts with decisions. Thank you to PacTrans for supporting this PacTrans Small Project. We welcome state transportation agencies' ideas and look forward to your questions.

The bridge profile adds useful forecasting information.

Earlier, larger model. Study removing one kind of bridge information: 3,000 bridges, 3 test groups. Weather remains a topic for study.

This study uses the earlier, larger model. It removes one kind of bridge information at a time, which the chart calls ablation. On a three thousand bridge sample with three test groups, the one-year error change is plus five point seven percent when only rating history is used. Leaving out the state changes error by plus six point one percent. Leaving out structural information changes it by plus four point one percent. Traffic and year built show smaller changes at one year. These comparisons describe how the bridge profile contributes to this model. Explaining the role of location and weather calls for further studies. This sample is separate from the full regional test.
